clue.text: Upset to be sacked?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: let down, saddened by an unmet hope
second meaning: removed from an appointment or post

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the word into dis- plus appointed, so someone stripped of their appointment has been sacked.
explanation.definitionFit: The everyday sense is let down; the punning sense undoes an appointment, as when an employee is dismissed.

clue.text: Lime fan fans fan

definitions.note: a verb here: to fan passions is to stir them up

indicators.note: to fan things is to spread or stir them about, so these letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Three fans in a row, as if a citrus enthusiast were waving at another admirer.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word does three jobs: noun inside the fodder, verb as the anagram signal, and verb again as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To fan anger or flames is to stoke and intensify them, which is exactly to provoke or arouse them.

clue.text: New capitals unable to develop properly

indicators.note: a new version of the word is a rearranged one, signalling that its letters are reshuffled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Newly founded capital cities that fail to grow as planned.
explanation.definitionFit: In medicine, aplastic describes tissue, such as bone marrow in aplastic anaemia, that fails to form or regenerate normally.

clue.text: History of divine gold leaves

indicators.note: gold leaves the divine, so those letters are taken out of the word

parts.note: a divine is a clergyman, such as a pastor
OR is the heraldic term for gold

explanation.surface: A history of the gold leaf used in religious art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gold leaves' reads as gilding, but leaves is a verb: the gold departs.
explanation.definitionFit: The past is what has already happened, the subject matter of history.

clue.text: Current decision-makers in court tip those unfit to take part

parts.note: in, as in fashionable or current
a jury decides the verdict in a trial
a ship that tips over to one side is said to list

explanation.surface: A jury in a trial reaching a fresh decision about someone's tip-off.
explanation.walkthrough: A list here is the verb for leaning, as a ship does.
explanation.definitionFit: A sports team's injury list names the players currently hurt and therefore unavailable for selection.

clue.text: Understood emperor to be missing us

indicators.note: the emperor is missing us, so those two letters are absent from his name

parts.note: Tacitus was a Roman emperor of the third century
taken as written

explanation.surface: A nostalgic sense that the emperor longs for our company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Missing us' reads as pining; here it means lacking the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tacit is implied without being stated, understood by everyone though never spoken aloud in words.

clue.text: Reproduction has gone wrong, leading to anger

parts.note: a dud is a fake, such as a counterfeit copy of a banknote

indicators.note: the letters of the word gone are put the wrong way round, into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Breeding has failed, and that failure leaves someone furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has gone wrong' reads as one verb phrase, but has is only a link and wrong works on the word gone.
explanation.definitionFit: Dudgeon is a feeling of deep resentment, usually in the phrase in high dudgeon, meaning offended indignation.

clue.text: Comedian toyed with gyrating to afford nose-job

indicators.note: spinning round, so the letters of the two words are whirled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A comedian fooled about by spinning round to pay for cosmetic surgery on his nose.
explanation.definitionFit: An adenoidectomy removes the adenoids at the back of the nasal passage, so it is literally surgery on the nose.

clue.text: Wine kit thefts managed to make things worse

indicators.note: the letters are handled and worked into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone stole home-brewing kits, and that only deepened the trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to aggravate someone's pain or distress, as turning a blade already in a wound would.

clue.text: Some of those life drawings displayed back passages

indicators.note: the run of letters is read from right to left
only part of the run of letters across these words is taken

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Life drawings that showed rear passages, a mildly risque gallery scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back passages' reads as one phrase, but back is the reversal signal and passages alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A defile is a narrow pass or gorge through which troops can march only in single file.

clue.text: Lift up, bundle over and crow

parts.note: to jack up a car is to raise it

indicators.note: turned over, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a wad is a bundle, as of banknotes

explanation.surface: Instructions for picking something up and parcelling it, ending with a boast.
explanation.walkthrough: Crow looks like a verb, to boast, but it is the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The jackdaw is a small grey-naped bird belonging to the crow family.

clue.text: New Listener crossword's crux gets closer

parts.note: an ear is what listens
the central letter of the nine-letter word crossword

explanation.surface: The heart of a new Listener puzzle is nearly solved.
explanation.walkthrough: The Listener is a famously hard weekly crossword in The Times, which makes the capital a misleading nudge.
explanation.definitionFit: To near something is to approach it, coming steadily closer in space or time.

clue.text: Annoy son describing radical siblings

indicators.note: in its old sense of drawing round, so these letters enclose another

parts.note: to bother someone is to annoy them
R is a standard abbreviation for radical in politics

explanation.surface: Irritating a son by talking about his militant brothers and sisters.
explanation.walkthrough: Describing is used in its geometric sense of tracing a line around something.
explanation.definitionFit: Brothers are male siblings, children of the same parents.

clue.text: Average dilettantes announced limits

indicators.note: spoken out, so the two words are heard as one word of similar sound

parts.note: par is the average or normal level and amateurs are dilettantes, so the phrase gives par amateurs

explanation.surface: Run-of-the-mill amateurs declaring the boundaries of their hobby.
explanation.definitionFit: Parameters are the set bounds within which something must operate, as in working within the parameters.

clue.text: Certain popular musical combo's fourth cover of Lucille

parts.note: in, as in fashionable
Evita is the Lloyd Webber musical about Eva Peron

indicators.note: the fourth letter of the word combo

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the outside letters of the name, which wrap round it like a cover

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A popular band's fourth single was a cover of the song Lucille.
explanation.walkthrough: Cover reads as a band's version of a song, which suits combo and Lucille, a Little Richard hit.
explanation.definitionFit: What is inevitable is bound to happen, a sure thing that cannot be avoided.

clue.text: Picked up idiot's tie

indicators.note: heard, so the word for the idiot is taken by its sound

parts.note: a nit is a fool, in British slang

explanation.surface: Someone collected a fool's necktie.
explanation.walkthrough: The K is silent, so the word for joining sounds exactly like the British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: To knit is to join or bind together, as broken bones knit or a close-knit family is bound.

clue.text: Italian jerk gets sentimental

parts.note: a Roman is an Italian from the capital
a tic is an involuntary twitch

explanation.surface: An Italian creep turns soppy.
explanation.walkthrough: Jerk reads as an insult for a person, but here it is a muscle spasm.
explanation.definitionFit: A romantic person is idealistic and given to tender, often sentimental, feeling.

clue.text: Celtic language introduction removed from poetry

indicators.note: the opening letter of the word for poetry is dropped

parts.note: verse is poetry

explanation.surface: A Gaelic language whose opening is taken out of a poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Erse is an old name for Scottish or Irish Gaelic, both members of the Goidelic branch of languages.

clue.text: Bone in back starts to undergo manipulation

parts.note: the stern is the back of a ship

indicators.note: the opening letters of each of the following words

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A spinal bone getting osteopathic treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: A bone in the back suggests the spine, but this bone is at the front of the chest.
explanation.definitionFit: The sternum is the breastbone, the flat bone at the front of the chest joining the ribs.

clue.text: Asian poet's surprisingly intense

indicators.note: the letters come out in an unexpected arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An Asian poet whose work is unexpectedly fervent.
explanation.definitionFit: Passionate feelings are strong and ardent, so the word fits intense as a description of emotion.

clue.text: When to stop hosts parking in bitumen?

indicators.note: these letters host another, holding it inside

parts.note: as in the sense of while or when
to halt is to stop
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: A question about when to stop when a host offers parking on the tarmac.
explanation.definitionFit: Asphalt is a dark mixture of bitumen with gravel used for road surfaces, and the word also names natural bitumen itself.

clue.text: Melancholy in Chelsea FC?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a state of low spirits
second meaning: the nickname of the London football club, which plays in blue

explanation.walkthrough: Chelsea FC is a London Premier League football club; its fans and players are known by its nickname from its blue shirts.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling low is having the blues, and the London club is nicknamed for its blue kit.

clue.text: Rose suddenly allowed to include American Pie's introduction

indicators.note: these letters take in others, holding them inside

parts.note: to let is to allow

indicators.note: the first letter of the following word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone jumped up when allowed to hear the opening of the song American Pie.
explanation.walkthrough: American Pie reads as Don McLean's song title, but American supplies one letter and Pie another.
explanation.definitionFit: To leap is to spring upward, so leaped means rose suddenly from the ground.

clue.text: A small enclosure for tree

parts.note: taken as written
a pen is a fenced enclosure for animals

explanation.surface: A small fenced patch set aside for a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The aspen is a poplar species known for leaves that tremble in the slightest breeze.

clue.text: A zip that is indigo

parts.note: taken as written
zip is slang for nothing, or nil

explanation.surface: A fastener coloured deep blue.
explanation.definitionFit: Anil is the indigo plant and the blue dye obtained from it, a crossword staple.

clue.text: Composite photo of Romeo, say, removing uniform?

indicators.note: taking off, so the letter for uniform comes out of the name

parts.note: Romeo is an example of a Montague, the family in Romeo and Juliet
U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A picture of an actor playing Romeo taking off his costume.
explanation.walkthrough: Uniform, after Romeo, belongs to the phonetic alphabet, which gives the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A montage is a picture assembled from several images, the essence of a composite photograph.

clue.text: Absolutely unspoilt Saharan cliffs occasionally seen

indicators.note: only now and then, so just every third letter of the words is used

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Pristine desert cliffs glimpsed now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: Not half is British slang for an emphatic yes: 'Did you enjoy it?' 'Not half!'
explanation.definitionFit: The British exclamation means very much indeed, an emphatic agreement equivalent to absolutely.

clue.text: Came across note about church dispatching bishop to get mineral

indicators.note: about means around, so the met-and-note pair goes around the church word with its letter removed

parts.note: to come across someone is to meet them, past tense met
te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

indicators.note: dispatching means getting rid of, so the bishop's letter is taken away

parts.note: a basilica is a large church
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: Someone stumbles on a memo about a church that has sent its bishop away, and ends up with a rock sample.
explanation.definitionFit: A metasilicate is a salt of metasilicic acid, and several occur naturally as minerals.
